fields.Front: Define key, superkey, candidate key, primary key and foreign key.
fields.Back:
Key: a combination of attributes (or one attribute) used to enforce that no two tuples are identical - 'forces each row to be unique, just like your student number'.
Superkey: ANY attribute set that enforces uniqueness.
Candidate key: a MINIMAL superkey - no proper subset of it is a superkey.
Primary key: the one candidate key WE pick; underlined; may be composite.
Foreign key: attributes in one relation matching the candidate key of some other (possibly the same) relation.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: SSN | LastName | FirstName with rows (34, Simpson, Homer), (56, Simpson, Marge), (78, Smithers, Marge), (99, Simpson, Homer). What is the key, and what fails?
fields.Back: SSN alone is the sensible key (and so are SSN+FirstName, SSN+LastName, or all three - those are superkeys). FAILS: LastName alone (three Simpsons); FirstName alone (two Homers, two Marges); and (LastName, FirstName) TOGETHER, because Homer Simpson appears in rows 1 and 4.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: the table LastName | FirstName holds Simpson Homer, Simpson Marge, Smithers Marge, Simpson Homer. What is the key?
fields.Back: There is NO key: rows 1 and 4 are identical - 'in Codd's version of the relational model this wouldn't even be allowed to happen'. If the last row were Smithers Homer, (LastName, FirstName) would be unique IN THAT SNAPSHOT, but she calls it 'just a snapshot in time' and 'not a good key': the next Homer Smithers hired would break it. Choose a key from the MEANING of the mini-world, not from which rows happen to be present.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: Attribute1|Attribute2|Attribute3 with rows (a1,b1,c1), (a1,b2,c1), (a2,b1,c2), (a2,b2,c2). Give the candidate keys, a superkey that is not a candidate key, and one pair that fails.
fields.Back: No single attribute works (a1, b1, c1 each appear twice). Candidate keys: (Attribute1, Attribute2) and (Attribute2, Attribute3). All three together form a SUPERKEY but not a candidate key - 'I didn't really need Attribute3', so it is not minimal. (Attribute1, Attribute3) FAILS: (a1, c1) appears in rows 1 and 2.

fields.Front: Car table (LicenseNum, EngineSerialNum, Make, Model, Year): give three superkeys, the candidate keys, and how the primary key is chosen.
fields.Back:
Superkeys: LicenseNum; EngineSerialNum; any combination containing one of them, e.g. (LicenseNum, Make). Make alone is not - it repeats.
Candidate keys: LicenseNum and EngineSerialNum. (Make, Model, Year) is not one - Ford Mustang 98 appears twice.
Primary key: 'it depends on the context' - to track who drives which car use LicenseNum; a mechanic or dealer would use EngineSerialNum. The slide chooses EngineSerialNum.

fields.Front: State the two key constraints, and say what scope they and referential integrity have.
fields.Back:
1. Keys must be UNIQUE (the key constraint).
2. The primary key must be NON-NULL - the ENTITY INTEGRITY constraint: 'you can never, ever put a null value in for a primary key'.
Most DBMSs enforce both automatically once you identify the primary key. These, with domain constraints, are constraints on a SINGLE table; referential integrity is the constraint BETWEEN tables.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: Department(DeptID, DeptName, MgrEmpID, MgrStartDate) and Employee(EmpID, LastName, FirstName, DeptID, Sex). Name the foreign keys, and is the mutual reference legal?
fields.Back: Employee.DeptID references Department.DeptID (Mike and Laura work in CompSci, 11); Department.MgrEmpID references Employee.EmpID (CompSci is managed by employee 003, Mike Bauer). Each table refers to the other, which is perfectly legal.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: you try to insert a row whose primary key is already present, and another whose primary key is blank. What does a DBMS do?
fields.Back: It refuses both. DBMSs enforce uniqueness and NOT NULL automatically, as long as you have identified the primary key. (Access reports 'duplicate values in the index, primary key, or relationship' for the first and 'You must enter a value' for the second.)

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §5.2.2): give the formal definitions of superkey and key, and the two properties a key must satisfy.
fields.Back:
SUPERKEY: a set of attributes SK such that for any two distinct tuples t1 and t2 in any state of R, t1[SK] != t2[SK]. That is a UNIQUENESS CONSTRAINT. Every relation has a default superkey - the set of ALL its attributes - because a relation is a set and cannot hold duplicates.
KEY: a superkey with the extra property that removing any attribute leaves a set that is no longer a superkey. So a key satisfies:
1. UNIQUENESS - superkeys have this too.
2. MINIMALITY - required for a key, OPTIONAL for a superkey.
Shortcut: any superkey formed from a SINGLE attribute is automatically a key; only multi-attribute keys need the minimality check.
A key is a property of the RELATION SCHEMA, must hold in every valid state, is TIME-INVARIANT (it must keep holding as tuples are inserted), and is determined from the MEANING of the attributes, not from the rows you happen to see.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §5.2.4): give the two formal conditions for a set of attributes FK in R1 to be a foreign key referencing R2, and name the two relations.
fields.Back:
1. The attributes in FK have the SAME DOMAIN(S) as the primary key attributes PK of R2 - which is why a foreign key column must have the same data type as the key it references.
2. A value of FK in a tuple t1 of the current state of R1 either OCCURS AS A VALUE OF PK for some tuple t2 in the current state of R2, OR IS NULL. In the first case t1[FK] = t2[PK] and we say t1 REFERENCES t2.
R1 is the REFERENCING relation; R2 is the REFERENCED relation.
A foreign key may reference its own relation: Super_ssn in EMPLOYEE references EMPLOYEE. The book draws each constraint as a directed arc from the foreign key to the primary key it references - which is what the Access Relationships window shows.

fields.Text: A {{c1::superkey}} is any attribute set that makes tuples unique; a {{c1::candidate key}} is a minimal superkey; the {{c1::primary key}} is the candidate key the designer chooses, signified by underlining it; a foreign key matches the candidate key of another (or the same) relation.

The rule that a primary key may never be null is the {{c1::entity integrity}} constraint; key and {{c1::domain}} constraints apply to {{c1::individual (single) tables}}, while referential integrity constraints apply between tables. On the slides, foreign keys are marked with an asterisk.

Textbook (Elmasri §5.2.2): NOTATION - Elmasri's word {{c1::key}} means what the slides call a {{c1::candidate key}} (a minimal superkey); the book uses 'candidate' only when a relation has more than one. The candidate keys not chosen as primary are called {{c1::unique keys}} and are not underlined.

Textbook (Elmasri §5.2.4): {{c1::key constraints and entity integrity}} are specified on an individual relation, whereas {{c1::referential integrity}} is specified between two relations. Entity integrity exists because NULL primary keys would mean {{c1::some tuples could not be identified or distinguished}} when referenced from other relations.
